About

I’m Finni Chang. I design visual systems, and my whole philosophy fits in three words: context is everything.

My path here was not a straight line. I started in research at UC San Diego. Then I spent a decade in games: art direction at Gaia Online, lead artist roles at Glu Mobile and Episode, building avatar systems and the teams behind them. I did a UI/UX program at Springboard in 2020, then joined Facebook to work on Avatars, and moved into Visual Systems at Meta in 2022. The scale changed at every stop. The work did not. Figure out the context first. Then build the system that fits it.

Product

I am a maker and an entrepreneur at heart, and my training is in science. I like inventive, resourceful fixes for complex problems, but I test them against reality. A team that works with me gets a designer who checks ideas against how products actually ship.

Strategy

I look for context in every scenario. The product, of course. Also the teams and pipelines around it. If something needs to scale, I build that into the foundation from the start. Bolting it on later rarely works.

Leadership

I think people do their best work in spaces where they feel safe enough to really try. A lot of my work is translation: helping people understand each other, and lining up what each person is good at with what the work needs, until things start to move.

Accessibility, from the start

I do not save accessibility for a checklist at the end. I think about it in two parts. The physical part is color, contrast, and motion: what can you actually see? The cognitive part is legibility, formatting, and cognitive load: what does it mean, and how hard is it to take in?

Contrast can be measured. WCAG does it mathematically. Color should never be the only way information gets across. Motion needs a still version, and images need alt text that says what the image was trying to say. Bigger does not always mean better, either: text packed in with no breathing room is harder to read than smaller text with margin around it.

The short version is this: information has to survive being seen differently. Different eyes, devices, environments, and levels of attention. If a message only exists in one form, it does not exist for everyone. I never assume other people are viewing my work under the same conditions and settings I am.

That applies to AI, too. Agents parse text first, so information should live in plain text, and images need a text transcription. The key to an accessible experience is simple: people need more than one way to get to the information in a visual.

AI, in its place

AI belongs in the work around the work. It does not belong in the creative call itself. A lot of a visual designer’s job is not making images. It is the layer around them: file naming, keywords, search, and metadata, where a human miss is expensive. AI also helps with accessibility work like alt text, where the gap is too large to close by hand.

The tools I built for this are specific. One is a Claude plugin, fb-asset-manager, which backfills descriptions, alt text, and keywords for the Meta Asset Manager. The other is AssetLookup, a Figma plugin that checks illustration containers against the Visual Asset Framework and recommends assets that already exist. I decide where the automation fits. I also decide where it does not.

Both tools are non-destructive by design. Review comes first, and nothing overwrites existing work. There are failsafes built in, like version control and automated backups, before anything is committed. Generated output is never final. A person reviews it, revises it, or rejects it. Whether something is good enough to ship stays a human judgment.
